title: Accompanying the dying
hookLine: being present, saying the Shema, holding a hand
tomorrow: after a loss, why does Jewish mourning hand you a schedule?

cards: A hospice hallway. Soft shoes, a cart going by, a door left half open. Somewhere inside, someone you love is near the end, and the question pounding in your chest is: what do I say?
Here's the gentle news from the tradition. The words matter less than you think. What matters is that you go in.

teach.b: When Jacob goes down to Egypt, God promises him in a dream that his son will be with him at the end: "and Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes." The promise isn't a speech. It's a hand.
Years later, Jacob dies surrounded by his sons, after speaking to each. Jewish custom carries that closeness forward.
Tradition asks that a dying person not be left alone.
Those with them may help them say a short confession, or say for them the line the prayer book sets for morning and night: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one."
And when no words come at all, a hand held is enough.

teach.h: THE WEEK MEETS IN THAT ROOM.
teach.b: Every line from this week meets in that room. The later years have their task, even now. You rise for the one in the bed.
Doctors and prayer, together. The carers there are holy. Values already passed on.
Wishes already known, so nobody is guessing.
All that's left is to be present.

how: Jewish custom asks that a dying person not be left alone; family or friends may help them say the Vidui, a short confession, and the Shema, or say it for them.

o: a prayer only clergy may say at a deathbed
a ceremony held only after someone has died
staying close to someone dying so they're not alone

games.q: this week, line by line — tap the pairs.
p: the surgeon and the Mi Sheberakh

s: only a rabbi may say the Shema with a dying person
family or friends may say it with them, or for them.
God promises Jacob that Joseph will put his hand on his eyes
Genesis 46:4: the promise is a hand, not a speech.
what a dying person needs most is the perfect words
tradition asks first that they not be left alone. a hand held is enough.

games.q: your friend's grandmother is in hospice. your friend says, "i don't go in. i never know what to say." what fits?
o: go in and sit; being present matters more than the words.
wait to visit until she's found the right thing to say.
send a card instead; visits are for close family only.
games.why: Joseph's promise was a hand on his father's eyes. tradition asks that the dying not be left alone; the words can be few, or none.

practice: If someone is with you, hold their hand, and say nothing. If you're alone, rest one hand inside the other and feel its warmth. Keep a person in mind, near or far, who needs someone beside them, and stay with them in your thoughts.

wordCard.voice: Accompanying the dying: staying close, saying the Shema or nothing at all, and holding a hand, so no one goes alone.

orig.note: Hebrew: hear. the first word of Hear, O Israel, said morning and night and at the end of life.

carryVoice: Your line: be present; a hand held says what words can't. Take good care of yourself tonight.
